title: What is CI/CD?
subtitle: Continuous Integration, Delivery, and Deployment — the philosophy and the pipeline

content.text: The 'works on my machine' problem — at scale

In the early 2000s, software teams integrated code once every few weeks — or months. Every integration was a painful, risky event: merge conflicts piled up, tests hadn't run in weeks, and the release process involved days of manual steps. Bugs that could have been caught in minutes festered for weeks. CI/CD was invented to solve this: make integration frequent, make testing automatic, and make deployment a non-event.
CI, CD (Delivery), CD (Deployment) — the three terms

content.definition: Every code push automatically triggers: build the project, run all tests, check code quality. If anything fails, the developer is notified immediately — while the context is fresh. Goal: always keep the main branch in a deployable state.

After CI passes, the code is automatically packaged and deployed to a staging environment, ready for production at the push of a button. The deployment to production is a manual trigger — but the process is fully automated.

Goes one step further: if all checks pass, code is deployed to production automatically — no human in the loop. This is what companies like Netflix, Etsy, and Shopify do — deploying hundreds of times per day.

content.title: Pipeline Stages — Interactive Flow
content.code:
CI/CD Pipeline Simulation
⚡
git push origin main
Developer pushes code → pipeline triggers automatically
1
Checkout & Install
PENDING
📥 Checkout code from repository
📦 npm ci (clean install from lock file)
💾 Cache node_modules for future runs
2
Test
PENDING
🧪 npm test (unit tests + integration)
📊 Generate coverage report
❌ Fail pipeline if coverage < 80%
3
Lint & Type Check
PENDING
🔍 ESLint — check code style and patterns
📝 Prettier — check formatting
🏷️ tsc --noEmit — TypeScript type checking
4
Build
PENDING
🏗️ npm run build (vite/webpack production build)
🐳 docker build -t myapp:$SHA .
📤 docker push to registry
5
Deploy to Staging
PENDING
🚀 Pull new image on staging server
🔄 docker compose up -d (rolling restart)
✅ Smoke test staging URL

content.text: Why CI/CD changes how teams work

items: Smaller, safer changes — when deploying is easy, you deploy often. Small changes are easier to review, test, and roll back.
Faster feedback — a bug caught in CI minutes after push is 10× cheaper to fix than one found in production weeks later.
No 'integration hell' — merging frequently means conflicts are small and frequent instead of large and catastrophic.
Confidence — developers can refactor fearlessly when tests run automatically on every push.

questions.question: What is the key difference between Continuous Delivery and Continuous Deployment?
options: Continuous Delivery uses Docker; Continuous Deployment does not
Continuous Delivery deploys to production manually after automated checks pass; Continuous Deployment deploys to production automatically
Continuous Delivery is for frontend apps; Continuous Deployment is for backend
They are the same thing — different teams just use different terms
questions.explanation: Continuous Delivery automates everything up to production — a human still clicks 'deploy to prod'. Continuous Deployment removes that final human gate — if all checks pass, it goes to production automatically. Both require high confidence in automated tests. Most teams start with Continuous Delivery and move toward Deployment as test coverage grows.

faq.q: Do I need CI/CD for my personal project?
faq.a: Yes — even a simple GitHub Actions workflow that runs tests and deploys on push saves time and prevents embarrassing bugs from reaching production. The setup takes 30 minutes and pays back immediately. Even a one-person project benefits from 'the tests passed' confidence before every deploy.
